node-1.label: A man in his 40s has multiple asymptomatic round hypopigmented macules symmetrically distributed on the face and neck for 2 years

node-2.label: The lesions appeared on his cheeks 2 years earlier and gradually coalesced

node-3.label: Physical examination showed multiple round, hypopigmented macules symmetrically distributed on the face and neck, ranging from 2-3 mm to 25 mm in diameter

node-4.label: There was no hair growth at the lesion sites, and the patient reported no symptoms

node-5.label: He was previously treated for tinea versicolor without success

why.why: The chronic symmetric hypopigmented macules and failed tinea treatment still suggest a hypopigmentary process, but the biopsy revealing a subepidermal epithelial tumor with clear cells and PAS-positive glycogen points to a specific benign adnexal neoplasm rather than a primary nonspecific hypopigmentary disorder. The absence of hair growth also made a nonspecific hypopigmentary disorder less likely, so confidence is reduced from 0.35 to 0.2.

Although symmetric hypopigmented macules with absent hair growth and failed tinea treatment initially supported leprosy, the pathologist's biopsy—the gold standard in this tumor-related differential—reveals a subepidermal epithelial tumor with clear cells and PAS-positive glycogen and is explicitly not leprosy. The laboratory physician's caution about pending confirmatory studies does not override this histologic evidence; slit-skin smear is unavailable, so leprosy cannot be absolutely excluded, but confidence is lowered from 0.45 to 0.08.

Tinea versicolor was already unlikely because prior treatment failed and the lesions are symmetric face/neck macules without hair growth. The biopsy additionally shows an epithelial tumor rather than fungal organisms, further refuting tinea versicolor, so confidence is reduced to 0.02.

node-9.label: Biopsy reveals a subepidermal epithelial tumor with clear cells and PAS-positive glycogen

node-10.label: Benign adnexal neoplasm (clear cell type) causing the hypopigmented macules

attrs.why: The biopsy finding of a subepidermal epithelial tumor with clear cells and PAS-positive glycogen is characteristic of a benign adnexal neoplasm, and the pathologist's interpretation explicitly favors this over leprosy. The symmetric facial/neck hypopigmented macules with absent hair growth may represent the clinical presentation of this neoplasm. Confidence is 0.6 because the pathologist advises clinical correlation, slit-skin smear is unavailable, and other hypopigmentary disorders have not been fully excluded by laboratory workup.
